title: Investigation breadcrumbs for regression triage
content:
Purpose: quick, repeatable breadcrumbs to follow when a performance alert (latency or error-rate) fires. This is an operational note for hot investigations — keep short, copyable commands, and heuristics to prioritize next actions.

Overview / intent:
- Provide a single-page checklist + triage heuristics we can run during pager events or async regressions.
- Document the small set of artifacts to collect for any downstream bisect or postmortem.
- Keep comparisons reproducible for canary vs baseline (how we pick cohorts / queries).

Immediate intake (first 10–15 minutes)
- Who: assign owner (usually oncall SRE + one serving runtime engineer).
  - Owner today: @oncall (SRE rotation) + eng-serving-runtime responder.
- Which alert: capture alert id, dashboard link, and query time window.
- Snapshot these values immediately (copy to incident thread):
  - metric: e.g., request_latency_p99_ms / request_error_rate
  - model(s) affected: model-id, model-version
  - region / pool / cluster name
  - start_time and end_time (UTC) for the anomaly window

Quick triage checklist (do in parallel):
- Dashboard quick checks (copy screenshots / permalinks):
  - p50/p90/p99 latency for the model(s) and global cluster over the time window
  - qps (successful requests/sec) and bursts (25/5m rate)
  - concurrency / inflight requests and queue length
  - GPU utilization and memory (%), CPU load on CPU-heavy paths
  - GPU temperature / ECC errors (if accessible)
  - System errors: OOM kills, container restarts, infra platform errors
  - Model-level errors: tokenization errors, decoding exceptions, model load failures

- Collect fast artifacts (commands you can run from runbook box):
  - dump one example request id and trace id (if available) from the dashboard
  - curl the request payload (redwood-cli get-request --id <reqid>)
  - fetch last 50 lines of the serving runtime logs for the instance(s): 
    kubectl -n rwd logs -l pool=<pool> --tail=200 | grep "<model-id>" -n --color=auto
  - grab a single flight recording (trace) around a slow request
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,temperature.gpu --format=csv -l 1 (for infra PVs)
  - dmesg | tail -n 200 (for kernel OOMs / driver faults)

Heuristics to classify initial root cause (fast eyeball rules):
- All models in pool slow + GPU util high and queued requests -> batching/backlog or throughput saturation.
- One model spike + GPU util low but CPU high -> CPU-side preprocessing or tokenizer hotpath regression.
- p99 spikes but p90 stable -> tail-latency regression (KV cache boundary, tokenization worst cases, locking)
- Error rate increased -> decoding exception, model crash, or incompatibility (inspect stack traces and model logs)
- Only one region affected -> network/region outage or regional infra change

Canary vs baseline comparisons (how we pick cohorts)
- Canary cohort selection: traffic routed to new revision (canary %) vs baseline revision. If rollout already happened, pick time windows where canary % changed.
- Golden traffic set: replay a small synthetic request set (~1000 requests) that we keep stable across comparisons (store in S3/benchdata). Use this for reproducible latencies.
- Bulk comparison approach: compute per-request latency delta -> histogram and CDF comparison. Prefer median of per-request diffs instead of separate medians.
- Automated checks to run: KS-test on latency distributions, bootstrap of mean/p99, and check that p99_canary - p99_baseline > threshold (threshold = 15% or +50ms absolute by policy).

Bisect plan (when suspected code change)
- If deploy timeline indicates a single image or infra change, do a binary rollback/bisect across deploys:
  1) Identify candidate images/releases between last-known-good and first-bad (from deploy history).
  2) If simple: rollback the canary to previous image and rerun golden traffic (fast smoke).
  3) If multiple commits between, use iterative bisect: split range in half, deploy midpoint revision to canary at 5% traffic, run smoke (golden) and compare.
  4) Automate comparison with a simple script: scripts/canary-compare.sh --baseline <rev> --candidate <rev> --bench s3://bench/golden-set.json -> outputs p50,p90,p99 deltas + hist plot link.
- When bisecting, always keep isolation rules: avoid mixing heavy production traffic that could affect user experience.

Profiling checklist if bisect suggests CPU or kernel issue
- Reproduce locally with smaller model or with a single-worker test harness.
- Capture perf flamegraph of the worker thread handling request: perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 30; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg
- Collect Python-level traces (py-spy or sampling profiler) for 30–60s around slow request
- If we suspect GPU kernel regressions, capture cupti traces or nvprof on a repro box (coordinate with infra team for dedicated GPU access)

Data to attach to ticket/postmortem (minimum required):
- Request ids (3 slow examples) + trace ids
- Per-model latency percentiles baseline vs incident
- Golden traffic output artifact and comparison script output
- Logs (serving runtime + model runner) clipped to time window
- Image / commit id + deployment timeline and rollout % changes
- Host metrics (nvidia-smi snapshot, top, vmstat, dmesg)

Quick commands / snippets (copy/paste)
- list recent deploys: rcli deploy list --cluster <cluster> --since 24h
- show canary traffic percent: rcli rollout status --model <model-id>
- force rollback to previous image: rcli rollout set --model <model-id> --image <image-id> --traffic 100
- run golden replay (on bench infra): ./scripts/replay_benchmark.py --target <endpoint> --input s3://bench/golden-set.json --concurrency 8 --out ./bench-output.json
- compare results: python ./scripts/compare_latencies.py --baseline ./baseline.json --candidate ./candidate.json --out ./diff-report.html

Owner & escalation matrix
- Triage owner: oncall SRE (initial), eng-serving-runtime responder (Ava / Marco / Priya rota)
- If GPU driver / kernel suspected: page infra-kernel team and escalate to infra-tech-leads
- If model-level regression (changed model weights or tokenizer): page model-ops + model-owner
- Security / data exfil concerns: follow security runbook (immediately notify Security)

Open questions / TODOs (investigation follow-ups)
- We need more automated canary-diff artifacts in the console: small histograms, delta plots per-model (ask product/console team)
- Add an endpoint to fetch a sampled set of raw request payloads for the last 24h (redwood-cli get-sample --model) — useful for reproducing tokenization regressions.
- Produce a standard golden-set per major model family (gpt-like, encoder-only) and commit to bench S3.

Post-incident actions (if regression confirmed)
- Create incident ticket with the artifacts list above and label with regression + severity
- Run the bisect to identify offending change and create revert PR if root cause is infra/kernel/driver
- If root cause is algorithmic (tokenizer/decoder), coordinate a patch and run benchmark suite across model versions
- Update this note with any novel heuristics learned (keep it living)

Appendix: quick heuristics table (text)
- Pattern: high p99 + high GPU util -> throughput saturation / batch sizing change.
- Pattern: high p99 + GPU util low + CPU spikes -> CPU preprocessing hotpath/regression.
- Pattern: increased tail + OOMs -> memory regression (quantization change, cache size change).
- Pattern: higher error rate + stack traces referencing "decode" -> decoding/tokenization bug in new model or tokenizer update.

Notes-to-self: keep screenshots and raw JSON outputs zipped and attach to Jira. When in doubt, revert to last-known-good deploy and collect time-windowed artifacts for offline bisect.

End of doc.
